headline: Tunify User's 400-Track Playlist Is Just One Song Repeated 400 Times
subheadline: Platform's 'Wrapped' report reveals 847 hours of identical listening
summary: A Tunify user's year-end listening report has gone viral for revealing extreme devotion to a single track.
content:
Tunify's annual "Wrapped" feature has revealed an extreme listener: user @OneTrackMind, whose 400-track playlist consists entirely of the same song repeated 400 times.

The song, "Dreams" by Fleetwood Mac, accounted for 847 hours of @OneTrackMind's listening time—approximately 35 days of continuous play. Their Wrapped report listed their top 5 songs as:

1. Dreams - Fleetwood Mac
2. Dreams - Fleetwood Mac
3. Dreams - Fleetwood Mac
4. Dreams - Fleetwood Mac
5. Dreams - Fleetwood Mac

"I like what I like," @OneTrackMind explained in a Chirper thread that went viral. "Why would I listen to other songs? This one's good. I know all the words. It never disappoints me. Other songs are a risk."

The post has sparked debate about musical consumption. Some defended the practice as "honest" and "knowing yourself." Others expressed concern about "algorithmic stagnation" and "refusing to grow."

Tunify's algorithm reportedly struggled with the user's account, unable to generate meaningful recommendations. "Based on your listening, you might enjoy: Dreams by Fleetwood Mac," read one suggestion.

"The algorithm tried to show me new music," @OneTrackMind reported. "I skipped everything. Eventually it gave up. Now it just recommends Dreams variations—live versions, covers, remixes. It adapted. I respect that."

Psychologists note that musical repetition is common and often comforting. However, 400 consecutive entries of one song "may exceed typical repetition patterns."

"There's 'comfort song' and then there's 'ritual,'" noted one expert. "This feels closer to ritual."

@OneTrackMind has announced plans to diversify their listening in the new year. "I'm thinking of adding one more song," they said. "Chain of Fools by Aretha Franklin. Just to mix it up. Maybe 50 times."

At press time, their playlist remained unchanged.
author: Alex Rivera, Digital Culture
